t: Minimize Manhattan Distances — Chebyshev Transform + Top-2 Extremes
o: Manhattan distance |x₁−x₂|+|y₁−y₂| equals max(|u₁−u₂|, |v₁−v₂|) where u = x+y and v = x−y. Hence the diameter of a point set is max(maxU − minU, maxV − minV). Removing one point only matters if that point is the unique achiever of one of these four extremes; otherwise the diameter is unchanged. So precompute the top-two maxima and top-two minima of u and v, then for each candidate removal substitute the runner-up where needed and evaluate the resulting diameter. Example 1: removing point (10,2) drops the diameter from 18 to 12.
k: Rotate coordinates: Manhattan diameter = max over u = x+y and v = x−y of (max − min).
Keeping top-2 max and top-2 min of each transformed coordinate lets us remove any single point in O(1).
Answer = min over all removals of the recomputed diameter; ties in extremes are handled automatically since the runner-up equals the max.

a.i: Compute (max1, max2, min1, min2) for arrays u and v. For each point r, the diameter without r is max(uMaxExcl(r) − uMinExcl(r), vMaxExcl(v) − vMinExcl(v)), where Excl picks the runner-up exactly when r holds the extreme. Take the minimum over r. This is O(n) versus the naive O(n²) of recomputing diameters.
s: Build u[i] = x+y, v[i] = x−y; extract top-2 maxima and minima of each.
For each i, compute the four extremes excluding i (swap in the second-best when i is the best).
Candidate = max(uMax − uMin, vMax − vMin); track the minimum candidate.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def minimumDistance(self, points: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(points)
        u = [x + y for x, y in points]
        v = [x - y for x, y in points]
        def top2(a):
            mx1 = mx2 = float('-inf'); mn1 = mn2 = float('inf')
            for x in a:
                if x > mx1: mx2, mx1 = mx1, x
                elif x > mx2: mx2 = x
                if x < mn1: mn2, mn1 = mn1, x
                elif x < mn2: mn2 = x
            return mx1, mx2, mn1, mn2
        M1, M2, m1, m2 = top2(u)
        N1, N2, p1, p2 = top2(v)
        ans = float('inf')
        for i in range(n):
            mu = M2 if u[i] == M1 else M1
            nu = m2 if u[i] == m1 else m1
            mv = N2 if v[i] == N1 else N1
            nv = p2 if v[i] == p1 else p1
            ans = min(ans, max(mu - nu, mv - nv))
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — two passes to find extremes, one pass to evaluate removals.
a.sp: O(n) — the transformed coordinate arrays (or O(1) if fused into one pass).

w: The Chebyshev rotation is the standard tool for Manhattan-diameter problems; commit it to memory. Tie-handling falls out naturally: if two points share the extreme value, the 'runner-up' equals it, so removing either leaves the diameter intact — exactly correct. Pitfall: coordinates up to 10⁸ mean u fits in 32 bits but differences are safer in 64-bit. Follow-up: remove k points (multiset of extremes / balanced BST), or maximize the minimum distance instead.
